Dark patterns (also called "deceptive patterns") = user interface designs that intentionally mislead or manipulate users into doing things they didn't really want to do—often benefiting the business instead of the user. (Wikipedia)

(coined): UX designer Person/Harry Brignull coined "dark patterns" (via darkpatterns.org, now rebranded as deceptive.design) to label interface designs that trick people into actions they wouldn't otherwise choose with full understanding. (Medium)

–present (research + governance lens): "Dark patterns" became a major topic in HCI research and policy discussions, increasingly framed as deceptive choice architecture—often using the same behavioral levers as Design/Persuasive, but aimed at outcomes that primarily benefit the business over the user. (ACM Digital Library)
Dark patterns sit on the manipulative end of the Design/Persuasive spectrum
They exploit cognitive biases (urgency, default bias, fear of missing out) to push users toward decisions that primarily benefit the business
Unlike ethical persuasive design, dark patterns prioritize business outcomes over user autonomy and understanding
A UX pattern in which documentation navigation shows the minimum product version that supports each feature, often as a compact label such as v0.17+.
Feature entries in a sidebar carry version metadata alongside their names.
The version label turns compatibility into part of feature discovery, so a reader can tell whether a feature is available in the version they use without opening a changelog.
secretspec uses this affordance in its website sidebar: scopes are marked as supported from v0.17+, while secret generation is marked as supported from v0.7+.

The pattern translates SemVer release history into an actionable compatibility signal. It helps readers choose a version baseline and understand when a feature entered the product without reconstructing that history from release notes.

Toggle Between the Current and Alternate File

You press Ctrl and 6. No Shift. ^ sits on the 6 key, and Ctrl with that key produces the character vim calls CTRL-^ — the name describes the character, not the keys, which is why it looks harder to type than it is. On some non-US layouts it is produced another way (:help CTRL-^).
